messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Fatima is a 51-year-old dentist of South Eastern Asian descent, married and living in a quiet suburban neighborhood. Two years ago, she was stalked by a former patient over a period of several months. The man would appear at her dental practice at odd hours, leave notes on her car windshield, and call the office repeatedly, sometimes disguising his voice. The stalking escalated when he began following her home, parking outside her house late at night. Fatima obtained a restraining order, but the man violated it twice before being arrested and incarcerated. Even after he was jailed, Fatima could not shake the feeling that he might return, or that someone else might take his place.

For months after the arrest, Fatima found herself unable to relax. She began to notice that certain songs on the radio—ones she had heard during the worst weeks of the stalking—would make her heart race and her palms sweat. When a news report or a true-crime podcast mentioned stalking, she would feel a surge of dread, as though the story were happening to her all over again. The moment a trigger appeared, she would scan the room for exits, check the locks on her doors, and feel a tightness in her chest that did not ease until she was in a space she controlled. She had come to believe that safety was an illusion, even when her husband told her the man was in prison. "You can't know for sure," she would say, "He could get out. He could have friends." No reassurance could penetrate the certainty she felt that danger was always near.

Fatima's daily life became a series of precautions. At work, she insisted on keeping her office door locked, and she positioned her chair so that her back was against the wall and she could see the entire room. When she walked into a restaurant or a waiting room, she automatically chose a seat with her back to a solid wall, avoiding tables in the center of the space. She had begun to avoid the news altogether, and she would change the radio station when a familiar song came on. Her husband noticed that she no longer wanted to go to the grocery store after dark, and she had stopped attending the community events she once enjoyed.

The causal connection between triggers and threat was tight and immediate. A single song on the radio could send her into a state of hypervigilance that lasted for hours. She would then spend the rest of the day checking the locks, scanning the driveway, and feeling a pervasive sense of unsafety that no amount of logic could counter. She had come to believe that the world was fundamentally dangerous, and that her own judgment—not anyone else's—was the only thing that could keep her alive. What frightened her most was the possibility that she would never feel safe again, that the man had stolen not just her peace of mind but her ability to trust in the ordinary safety of her life. She finally sought help when she realized she was beginning to dread going to work, the one place she had always felt competent and in control.
